blocks.html: How is data sent without getting lost? Data crosses a network in small numbered pieces called packets. Routers pass the packets along, and the receiver rebuilds the message in order.

items: Explain how packet switching divides, routes and reassembles a message.
Describe how routers forward packets and choose other routes.
Tell hostnames, IP addresses and DNS apart, and check if an IP address is valid.
Name common protocols and what they do.
I can draw the packet switching, routing and DNS algorithms as flowcharts.
I can use correct networking words in full sentences.

blocks.html: Packet switching splits a message into small, fixed-size, numbered packets. Each packet travels across the network, maybe by a different route, so packets can arrive out of order (2, 3, 1). The receiver uses the numbers to put them back in order.

blocks.alt: A message split into packets, sent through the Internet and reassembled

blocks.html: A message split into packets, sent through the Internet and reassembled
Each packet has a header with the sender and receiver addresses. If one packet is lost, only that packet is sent again.
Analogy: posting a book as three numbered envelopes. Each may travel a different way; you rebuild the book by number.
A router is a device that forwards packets toward their destination.

items: Read and forward: it reads the destination address and sends the packet to a directly connected router.
Next step only: no router knows the whole path, only the next best step.
Reroute: if a path is busy or blocked, it uses an alternative route. This makes the Internet fast and reliable.

blocks.html: Many users share the same lines at once because packets from different messages take turns.
Every computer on the Internet needs a unique address.

rows: Readable name, words separated by dots (for humans)
Four numbers 0 to 255 separated by dots (for routers)
head: Term
What it is
Example

blocks.html: It needs exactly four numbers, each from 0 to 255 (each fits in 8 bits).
This format is IPv4. The longer IPv6 format is used as IPv4 addresses run out.
The Domain Name System (DNS) is the Internet's phone book. It turns (resolves) a hostname into its IP address automatically.
Your computer saves recent answers in a cache, so it does not need to ask the DNS server every time.
A protocol is a set of rules for how data is formatted, sent and processed, like a shared language between computers.

rows: Rules behind packet switching on the Internet
head: Protocol
Job

blocks.html: The OSI model shows the layers where protocols work. TCP/IP came from DARPA research in the 1970s and was first used on ARPANET.
How a message is sent in packets and rebuilt.

steps: Is a packet missing? Yes: ask the sender to resend it, then collect again.
No: put packets in order and join.

steps: Is the destination directly connected? Yes: deliver the packet, then Stop.
No: choose the next best router.
Is that path busy or blocked? Yes: choose an alternative router.

steps: Check the cache for the IP.

labs.title: Week 11 Lab 1: The Web, URLs and Firewalls

blocks.html: Part 1 showed how packets, routers and DNS move data. This part shows how the Web uses the Internet, how to read a URL, and how a firewall keeps your computer safe.

items: Tell the Internet and the World Wide Web apart.
Name the three parts of a URL.
Explain what a firewall does and name its three generations.
Check that Windows Defender Firewall is on.
I can draw how a web page opens and how a firewall decides, as flowcharts.
I can explain why a firewall matters on public Wi-Fi.

blocks.html: They are not the same: the Web is one service that runs on top of the Internet.

rows: A global network that lets connected computers talk to each other
A system of linked web pages reached over the Internet
The medium: cables, routers and devices
Uses the HTTP protocol; pages are written in HTML
Carries email, file transfer, games, video calls and the Web
Read in web browsers; pages are joined by hyperlinks
head: The Internet
The World Wide Web

blocks.html: Analogy: the Internet is the road system; the Web is the buildings you visit, joined by signposts (hyperlinks).
The Web was invented by Tim Berners-Lee, who made the first HTTP communication in 1989.
A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the address of a web page.

rows: The rules used to transfer the page
Names the host; DNS finds its IP address
Finds the exact page on that host
head: Part
What it does

blocks.alt: A web page and the HTML code the browser reads

blocks.html: A web page and the HTML code the browser reads

A firewall is a security barrier between your computer or local network (LAN) and the Internet. It checks packets and decides which to allow and which to block. It can be software on your computer, part of a router, or a separate device.

blocks.alt: The firewall filters traffic between the Internet and the LAN

blocks.html: The firewall filters traffic between the Internet and the LAN
Why it matters: on public Wi-Fi (cafes, airports, malls) strangers share your network, so a firewall blocks unwanted connections. Use it together with antivirus, strong passwords and updates.

rows: Checks each packet against rules set by the network owner
Holds packets until it can judge the connection: new, existing, or not part of one
Understands FTP, DNS and HTTP, and rejects anything strange or abused
head: Generation
How it works

blocks.html: Each generation is smarter: from simple rules, to remembering connections, to understanding what the data means.

items: Search for Control Panel and open it.
Green shields mean the firewall is on.
If it is off, click Turn Windows Defender Firewall on or off.
Choose Turn on for private and public networks, then click OK.

blocks.alt: Turn on the firewall for both network types, then click OK

blocks.html: Turn on the firewall for both network types, then click OK
What happens from typing a URL to seeing the page.

steps: Split the URL into its parts (protocol, hostname, path).
Get the IP address using DNS.
Server sends the HTML page (in packets).
Is a hyperlink clicked? Yes: take the link's new URL and go to step 3.

blocks.html: How a firewall decides about each packet.

steps: Part of an existing allowed connection? Yes: ALLOW the packet.
No: does a rule allow it? Yes: ALLOW the packet.
No: BLOCK the packet and log it.
Are there more packets? Yes: go to step 2.

blocks.html: How to make sure your firewall is switched on.

steps: Are all the shields green? Yes: go to step 7.
No: click "Turn firewall on or off".
Turn on for private and public networks, then click OK.
